newsitem.title: USA: EVEN IN DEATH, ELVIS LIVES.
newsitem.headline: EVEN IN DEATH, ELVIS LIVES.

text.p: Who says the King is dead?
As millions of fans prepare to mark the 20th anniversary of Elvis Presley's death on Saturday, the spirit of the man who changed the sound of music lives on.

Across the United States, fans will mark the anniversary in almost every conceivable way, from listening to radio stations playing "Hound Dog" and other hits non-stop to watching TV specials, including one called "Elvis Meets Nixon," to making claims they just saw the King of Rock'n'Roll at the supermarket.

But nowhere will the celebrations be as big or as feverish as in Memphis, Tennessee, where Elvis built his castle, called it Graceland and died in 1977 at the age of 42 of a drug-induced heart attack.

Memphis, which declared an Elvis week, is bracing for 50,000 fans for what is billed as the biggest Elvis extravaganza ever -- bigger even than his 1977 funeral attended by thousands of hysterical fans, many of whom were overcome by grief and sweltering heat.
There will be Elvis riverboat cruises and dance parties and the dedication of a new statue at the Elvis restaurant.

Fans can quiz the King's friends about his life, meditate at his grave, run in an Elvis Presley International race, tour his parents' Graceland bedroom for the first time or share memories with hairdresser Larry "Confidant to the King" Geller.
Geller loves to tell how he coiffed the dead King's hair and dyed it black with mascara to get rid of every grey strand. "I did it for Elvis," he says.
A bevy of Elvis impersonators will be on hand asking young women to "Love Me Tender" and warning their boyfriends not to step on my "Blue Suede Shoes."
VIDEO ELVIS TO PERFORM LIVE CONCERT

The high point of the week will be the use of technology to bring Elvis back to life for an "Elvis In Concert '97" stage performance. Video wizards will blend film of Elvis in concert with a new on-stage performance by the now ageing and in some cases pot-bellied musicians he used to play with.

Born in a shack in Tupelo, Mississippi, Presley started his hit-making in 1954 with his version of "That's All Right." Over the next 23 years he racked up hit after hit, selling more than 1 billion records worldwide.
There was an Elvis for every occasion: Elvis the Pelvis, Elvis the Rocker, Army Elvis, Movie Elvis, Leather Elvis, Las Vegas Elvis and, finally, Fat Elvis.

Elvis had so many different looks that when the U.S. Postal Service decided to issue an Elvis stamp in 1993 a national debate ensued over whether to use a young Elvis or a overweight jump-suited Elvis on the imprint. Young Elvis won.
He was credited for a teenage rebellion in the 1950s and helped break down barriers between black and white music. He even made sideburns trendy.

Now, more than four decades after his music was denounced as "evil" and his pelvis shaking called perverted, Elvis is still worshipped by fans with an almost spiritual devotion. For his most ardent fans a trip to Graceland can mean more than a trip to Lourdes or Bethlehem.
SCHOLARS LOVE ELVIS, TOO

The King is also revered by scholars, who will gather in Memphis to mark the anniversary of his death with the Third Annual International Conference on Elvis Presley. Organised by the world's self-styled "greatest living Elvis expert," Dr. Vernon Chadwick, the conference examines the King's influence on everything from politics to culture and religion.

Among topics on the conference agenda are "Elvis Presley and the Elasticity of Gender" and "Suspicious Minds: The Politics of Elvis Studies." On Thursday, the founder of the First Presleytarian Church of Elvis, Reverend Mort, will speak on the topic "What Really Happened in Bethlehem."
For Chadwick, 44, Elvis makes the perfect research topic. "He is a hero in an age that is lacking heroes," Chadwick said in an interview.

"Elvis sightings are the popular culture equivalent to the longing for ... mythical figures and especially religious martyrs. Not to be blasphemous but the first Elvis sighting was perhaps Jesus Christ after the resurrection," Chadwick said.

Some cultural historians argue Elvis may be bigger in death than in life. They cite as evidence that some 700,000 tourists and adoring fans flock each year to Graceland, fuelling a cottage industry of kitsch that sells everything from 35-cent postcards to $12,000 jukeboxes -- with the King's face on every item.
But the sad truth lies in the line used to end each concert by the King. As fans cheered for more, a voice would announce: "Ladies and Gentlemen, Elvis has left the building."
